• Reflection (reflection on the Cartesian plane along the x-axis, y-axis, lines parallel to the axes, y = x and y = −x)

records.why: KICD names two core competencies for this sub-strand (Learning to Learn; Creativity and Imagination). The unit listed five others that are not in KICD for this sub-strand. Restored the KICD sentences verbatim and tied each to a real activity in the lessons (guideline 2: tied to activities, not just listed).
records.value:
• Learning to Learn: the learner applies the properties of reflection to generate the image of an object on a given mirror line. In this unit: learners discover the coordinate rules from their own tables (Lessons 2-4), use them to predict images, check them by measuring, and correct their own work in their cumulative model.
• Creativity and Imagination: the learner locates the image of an object placed at a point in front of a mirror. In this unit: learners predict where the reflection of the boat lands in the flat-mirror demonstration (Lesson 1) and design a symmetrical pattern (Lesson 8, Task A).
records.reference: KICD Grade 10 curriculum design, Mathematics, Strand 2.0 Measurements and Geometry, Sub-Strand 2.2 Reflection and Congruence
records.old:
• Communication and Collaboration: Learners discuss and justify their reasoning about lines of symmetry, reflection transformations, and congruence conditions with peers during group activities and class presentations.
• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: Learners analyse Cartesian graphs to determine mirror lines, apply congruence conditions to unknown figures, and solve multi-step real-life problems involving reflections.
• Creativity and Imagination: Learners design symmetrical patterns inspired by Kenyan kitenge/ankara fabric, Maasai beadwork, and architectural motifs, applying reflection and congruence principles.
• Digital Literacy: Learners engage with videos and simulations on the ARES platform to observe reflections dynamically, building fluency with digital mathematical tools.
• Self-Efficacy: Learners build confidence by progressing from familiar symmetry (lines of symmetry) to formal congruence proofs, celebrating incremental mastery at each lesson phase.

records.why: The proof jumped from 'every point and its image are the same distance from the mirror line' straight to 'therefore every side length is preserved'. Equal distances from the line only say where each point lands; they do not by themselves give the length of a side (and SSS then needs those lengths as input). The explanation now uses the fold (the image lands exactly on the original) and the coordinate rules (for each mirror line in the unit the distance formula gives the same value for the image: for y = k only the vertical difference changes sign, for x = k only the horizontal difference does, for y = x the two differences swap, for y = −x they swap and change sign), then calls this 'rigid' and uses SSS. Checked: the distance formula is built from the squares of the two coordinate differences, and these four rules only swap or negate them, so the distance is unchanged.
records.old: when a shape is reflected across any straight line, every point and its image are the same distance from the mirror line. Therefore every side length is preserved. If all three sides of a triangle in the original equal all three sides of the corresponding triangle in the image, SSS guarantees congruence.
records.new: when a shape is reflected across a straight line, every point moves straight across the mirror line to the same perpendicular distance on the other side. So if we fold along the mirror line, the image lands exactly on the original, and the distance between any two points does not change (for the mirror lines in this unit the coordinate rules show it: for y = k only the vertical difference between two points changes sign, so the distance formula gives the same value). A transformation that keeps all distances is called rigid. So each side of the image triangle equals its partner in the original, and SSS guarantees congruence.
records.group_headline: The proof that a reflected image is congruent skipped a step (equal distance from the mirror does not on its own give equal side lengths); now it uses the fold and the coordinate rules, then SSS
records.reference: Euclid, Elements Book I (congruence of triangles, SSS); H. S. M. Coxeter, Introduction to Geometry (reflection as an isometry, mirror line as perpendicular bisector of point-image segments)

records.why: Same missing step as the Lesson 7 proof: 'reflection preserves perpendicular distances and therefore all three side lengths' does not follow. Now says the reflection moves each point straight across the mirror line so folding lays the image on the original.
records.old: because reflection preserves perpendicular distances and therefore all three side lengths.
records.new: because reflection moves every point straight across the mirror line, so folding along the waterline lays the image exactly on the original and each side matches its partner (all three side lengths are equal, which is SSS).
records.reference: Euclid, Elements Book I (congruence of triangles, SSS); H. S. M. Coxeter, Introduction to Geometry (reflection as an isometry)

records.why: Same fix: Part C now has students fold along the waterline and measure matching sides before naming SSS, instead of asserting equal lengths.

records.old: Phase 1 (Teacher demonstration — 5 minutes): Teacher holds a card cut-out of a boat shape against a flat mirror placed horizontally on the document camera or desk. Students observe how the image appears on the other side of the mirror surface, at what appears to be the same distance. Teacher moves the boat closer and further from the mirror and asks: 'What do you observe about the image as I move the boat?' Students respond chorally or with hand signals (thumbs up: image gets closer to mirror too; thumbs down: image stays in place). Phase 2 (Hands-on folding — 12 minutes): Each group receives three pre-cut card shapes: a Nile tilapia fish outline, a simplified dhow boat silhouette, and an acacia leaf outline. Students fold each shape trying to make the two halves match exactly. For each successful fold they draw the fold line with a pencil and label it 'Line of Symmetry.' Students record results in a simple table: Shape, Number of Lines of Symmetry Found, Sketch of the Line(s). Phase 3 (Video — 3 minutes): Teacher plays a short pre-prepared video showing lines of symmetry in Kenyan objects: a Maasai beaded collar, a kikoi fabric pattern, the outline of Mount Kenya, and the Kenyan coat of arms shield
records.new: Phase 1 (Teacher demonstration — 3 minutes): Teacher holds a card cut-out of a boat shape against a flat mirror placed horizontally on the document camera or desk. Students observe how the image appears on the other side of the mirror surface, at what appears to be the same distance. Teacher moves the boat closer and further from the mirror and asks: 'What do you observe about the image as I move the boat?' Students respond chorally or with hand signals (thumbs up: image gets closer to mirror too; thumbs down: image stays in place). Phase 2 (Hands-on folding — 10 minutes): Each group receives five pre-cut card shapes: a Nile tilapia fish outline, a simplified dhow boat silhouette, an acacia leaf outline, a rectangle and a parallelogram (not a rectangle). Students fold each shape trying to make the two halves match exactly, and also test folding the rectangle along a diagonal. For each successful fold they draw the fold line with a pencil and label it 'Line of Symmetry.' Students record results in a simple table: Shape, Number of Lines of Symmetry Found, Sketch of the Line(s). Phase 3 (Video — 3 minutes): Teacher plays a short pre-prepared video showing lines of symmetry in Kenyan objects: a Maasai beaded collar, a kikoi fabric pattern and the Kenyan coat of arms shield

records.old: The three shapes are carefully chosen for increasing complexity: the fish has one line, the boat has one line, and the acacia leaf can stimulate debate about whether it has exactly one or approximately one (introducing the idea that mathematical symmetry is exact, unlike natural objects).
records.new: The five shapes show one, two and no lines of symmetry: the fish and the boat have one line each, the rectangle has two, the parallelogram has none, and the acacia leaf can stimulate debate about whether it has exactly one or approximately one (introducing the idea that mathematical symmetry is exact, unlike natural objects). The rectangle's diagonal is the key misconception test: it cuts the rectangle into two congruent halves, but folding along it does not make them match, so a diagonal is not a line of symmetry.

records.why: The activity sheet is not in the data, so a teacher could not check answers, and the five steps (gradient and y = mx + c) do not apply to the horizontal and vertical items, which also made 20 minutes too short for three full constructions. Added a worked answer key with a sample sheet, the horizontal/vertical shortcut, and a no-compass method (fold so K lands on K′: the crease is the mirror line). Checked the sample: reflection in y = x + 1 is (x, y) → (y − 1, x + 1); K(1,4)→(3,2), L(3,6)→(5,4), M(1,6)→(5,2); midpoints (2,3), (4,5), (3,4) all satisfy y = x + 1; each segment has gradient −1, perpendicular to the mirror line of gradient 1.

records.new: At the 15-minute mark of Part B, issue a 5-minute warning and ask all pairs to ensure they have written at least one full equation. Answer key for a sample Activity Sheet 5 (use it if you draw your own sheet): (i) K(1, 4), L(3, 6), M(1, 6) with images K'(3, 2), L'(5, 4), M'(5, 2); midpoints of KK', LL', MM' are (2, 3), (4, 5), (3, 4); gradient between two midpoints = 1; substituting (2, 3) gives c = 1; the mirror line is y = x + 1. For items (ii) and (iii) the gradient method is not needed: the bisector of each segment is horizontal (y = c, gradient 0) or vertical (x = k, no gradient), so learners write the equation from the common midpoint coordinate, for example P(1, 2) and P'(1, 6) give y = 4, and E(2, 1) and E'(8, 1) give x = 5. Pairs do the five steps for item (i) only and write (ii) and (iii) directly, which keeps Part B within about 20 minutes. No compass? Fold the grid sheet (or a tracing-paper copy) so that K lands on K'; the crease is the mirror line; read two points on it to find the gradient.

Task 3 recomputed: P(2,3), Q(5,3), R(5,7): PQ = 3, QR = 4, PR = √(9 + 16) = 5; the reflection in the y-axis gives P′Q′ = 3, Q′R′ = 4, P′R′ = 5 (same three lengths); the angle at Q is a right angle so RHS also works. Look-fors and sample answers: Task 1 — the shared strut is a side of both triangles, so it counts as an equal pair ('BD = BD, common side'); forgetting the common side is the most frequent error. Task 2 — SAS needs the angle BETWEEN the two given sides; if the angle is not between them the proof is incomplete. Task 3 — PQ = 3, QR = 4, PR = √(3² + 4²) = 5 and P'Q' = 3, Q'R' = 4, P'R' = 5, so triangle PQR ≅ triangle P'Q'R' by SSS (RHS also works because the angle at Q is a right angle). Checked: Task A reflection in y = x swaps coordinates, (1,3)→(3,1) etc.; the midpoint of (1,3) and (3,1) is (2,2), on y = x, and the distance from (1,3) to the line is one grid-square diagonal, √2; Task B: triangles ABD and ECD have right angles at B and C, BD = CD and vertically opposite angles at D, so ASA gives CE = AB; Task C: reflection in x = 7 gives (14 − x, y): (2,1)→(12,1), (5,1)→(9,1), (5,4)→(9,4).
records.old: are identified for the exit task scaffolding support.
records.new: are identified for the exit task scaffolding support. Sample answer key (use it if you draw your own sheets): Task A — half-pattern points (1, 3), (2, 5), (1, 4), (3, 6), (2, 4) give images (3, 1), (5, 2), (4, 1), (6, 3), (4, 2); for (1, 3) and (3, 1) the midpoint (2, 2) lies on y = x and each point is one grid-square diagonal from the line. Task B — A is a tree on the far bank, B is opposite it on the near bank; C is on the near bank with BC at right angles to AB; D is the midpoint of BC; from C walk at right angles to BC to E, in line with A and D. Triangles ABD and ECD are congruent by ASA (right angles at B and C, BD = CD, vertically opposite angles at D), so CE = AB; if CE = 35 m the gorge is 35 m wide. Task C — left wing (2, 1), (5, 1), (5, 4) should give (12, 1), (9, 1), (9, 4) in x = 7; a right wing with (9, 5) instead of (9, 4) IS NOT congruent to the left wing.
records.reference: Euclid, Elements Book I (congruence of triangles, ASA); KICD Grade 10 curriculum design, Mathematics 2.2 (real-life applications of reflection and congruence)

records.why: Answer (4) said the image of every point can be predicted 'given the line of reflection in the form y = mx + c', but the unit only teaches coordinate rules for y = k, x = k, y = x and y = −x, plus the perpendicular-distance construction for any line. Reworded so it claims only what was taught.
records.old: (4) Yes — given the line of reflection in the form y = mx + c, every point of the image can be predicted exactly.
records.new: (4) Yes — once the line of reflection is known (for example y = k, x = k, y = x, y = −x, or any line found as in Lesson 5), every point of the image can be located exactly by going the same perpendicular distance to the other side.

records.why: The supporting phenomena named the wrong lessons: the matatu map is used in Lesson 3 (Lesson 2 uses the boat and Lesson 4 the tiles) and the Mombasa tiles in Lesson 4 (Lesson 5 is finding the mirror line).
records.old:
Reflecting a Matatu Route Map on a Grid (Lessons 2–4 — Cartesian Reflections): A simplified Nairobi matatu route map is plotted on a Cartesian grid; students observe how reflecting the map across the x-axis, y-axis, and parallel lines produces a "mirror-city" and investigate which landmarks land where.
• Mosque Geometric Tiling — Mombasa Old Town (Lesson 5 — y = x and y = −x Reflections)

records.why: The printed headings of the rubric are fixed by the template (the contract has three level fields), so the CBE level names Exceeds, Meets and Approaches Expectations are now written at the start of each descriptor, and the congruence descriptor now also asks for the reason the matching sides are equal (consistent with the corrected proof). Meaning of the other descriptors is unchanged.

value.criterion: Explaining reflection as the rule the water follows
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: clearly states that every point and its image are the same perpendicular distance from the line of reflection, links this to the same size of the image, and gives correct coordinate rules.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: states the equal-distance idea and gives the rule for the x-axis, but the link to the same size is not fully explained.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: says the image looks the same but gives no rule or no mention of equal perpendicular distance.

value.criterion: Accuracy of reflection calculations and the mirror line equation
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: all images are correct for every mirror line and the mirror line is found correctly as a perpendicular bisector, with working shown.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: most images are correct, and the mirror line is found with small errors in working.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: several images are wrong or the mirror line is not found.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: names SSS, explains why the matching sides are equal (the image lands exactly on the original when folded), lists all three pairs of equal sides, writes the congruence statement in correct vertex order, and names the other four conditions.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: names the condition and writes the statement but leaves out a step or a condition.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: does not name a correct condition or does not give a congruence statement.

value.criterion: Use of evidence and mathematical vocabulary
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: uses line of reflection, perpendicular distance, image, congruence and y = mx + c correctly, and supports claims with values from class work.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: uses most of the terms correctly, with some claims given without evidence.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: uses few terms or uses them incorrectly, with little evidence.

value.criterion: Connecting to the phenomenon and real life
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: gives a complete explanation of the Lake Victoria mirror image and a correct Kenyan application with clear reasoning.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: explains the mirror image and gives an application, but the reasoning is incomplete.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: gives a partial explanation, or an application with no reasoning.

records.why: CBE asks for four levels (Exceeds, Meets, Approaches, Below Expectations), but the partner contract allows only three level fields, so a 'Below Expectations' level cannot be represented in the current data. Suggested: teachers treat work that does not reach 'Approaches Expectations' as Below Expectations; or ask the partner to allow a fourth field.
